the-scale: Summer of 2022 I went to the doctor for chest pain, a pulled pec minor, and stepped on the scale: 240. I had never seen that number. Erin's second spinal fusion was a few weeks out and she would need all of me, so I built the most boring diet I could: chicken, broccoli, butter, bought in bulk, adaptation done before her surgery. I never set a target weight. That turned out to matter.
the-shamrock: On January 2nd, 2012, I ran about a mile, with Erin five months pregnant with Fiona. My oldest friend Craig was running the Shamrock Half Marathon in Virginia Beach, and if I was going to run it I was going to beat him. I picked a training program and followed it through snow, thirty-six missed calls the day Maddie broke her arm, and what looked like shin splints two weeks before race day.
feelings-are-data: Driving Alannah home from college, she got a text from an ex and went quiet, and I started trying to fix it. Not for her, for me. Young men get three emotional settings, fine, angry, and fix it now, and I ran that operating system for decades. The Body Keeps the Score, my father leaving when I was four, and a mistimed tuition payment showed me what the alarm in my chest is.
the-chaos-test: I started the chicken-and-broccoli system early so keto adaptation would be done before Erin's three-level spinal fusion. Then Ella FaceTimed from the rugby field at Christopher Newport at 10:30 on a Thursday night. Concussion, then four skull fractures, then a weekend waiting on an OR at VCU. A couple of weeks later Erin went under, and I found out my reserve of handle-it was finite. The containers of chicken just moved buildings.
the-loss-of-leadership: I beat the original Legend of Zelda at ten, and I still chase that feeling. Twenty years of coding was the adult version. Then I stopped writing code to lead, and for eighteen months I went home every day feeling like I hadn't produced anything. A phrase, a one-year-old Fiona smacking a spoon of peas out of my hand, and one whiteboard in front of a new CEO changed how I scored a day.
the-thinking-partner: I talk too fast for most people, and I've spent my life downshifting so they can keep up. A cognitive assessment explained why: a sports car engine bolted to a stock transmission. For decades my real system was bouncing ideas off friends, coworkers, Erin, and overwhelming all of them. Then I tried Claude, it pushed back, and I started talking to it through Wispr Flow at 142 words a minute. The bandwidth finally matched.
meet-claude: Early on, my chats with Claude ran long, and every time he'd start losing details and answering things I didn't say. It reminded me of my daughter the night she fractured her skull at rugby: nodding, but the lights flickering. He wasn't broken, he was overloaded. The opposite failure is just as bad: 'make this better' with no context. Here's what a context window actually is, and the one habit that fixes both.
the-garage-gym: In 2013 my testosterone came back at 300. The gel made me nervous with four daughters in the house, so I bought Craigslist plates and a $300 squat rack and ran StrongLifts until the number hit 400. Then I quit, and the equipment sat for eight years. On November 14th, 2022, I started over from the bar with no number to hit. Then came a hamstring tear, a hernia, and Alannah hitting a parked car.
totaling-the-prius: I bought a Prius in June 2006 for the HOV plates, because I was commuting ninety miles each way from Richmond to Gratis Internet in D.C. Thanksgiving week I dropped my water bottle in the 12th Street Tunnel and caused a three-car pileup. Six stitches at George Washington Hospital, then I was standing outside in a blood-soaked pink shirt with no coat, my office above the Macy's at Metro Center. So I went shopping.
disagree-and-commit: February 2023, the evening after my first colonoscopy, with instructions not to make major life decisions, Erin showed me puppies dumped in the woods in Blackstone, Virginia. My gut said bad idea. We already had Montana and Oliver the cat. The next morning I called her and said I'd disagree and commit, on two conditions: I train him and I name him. Then I built the system, starting with Monday weigh-ins at 17.3 pounds.
freeipodscom: For three weeks I slept with my laptop because freeiPods.com was buckling under traffic and I was the one holding it up. Fewer than twenty of us at Gratis Internet ran a dozen sites on a platform I built, climbed to 18th on the Inc. 500, and I got paid like it would last forever. In 2009 the founders sat me down. I took a two-thirds pay cut to stay in Richmond.
a-house-to-live-in: I built an AI agent called Bob one evening, talking to my phone while running errands. A few weeks later I built the better version and never saw Bob again. That's the pattern: Legos as a kid, twenty years of software, a crew of agents named after the Rocinante, all built and handed off. There's one house you can't hand the keys to, and for a long time I just didn't build it.
claude-chat-claude-code-and-me: I dictate through Wispr Flow and neither Claude Chat nor Claude Code survives transcription, so I gave them names from The Expanse. Amos for the brainstorm chat, Naomi for Claude Code, then Holden to coordinate and Alex, running on ChatGPT, to review. Along the way I wired every session to a shared GitHub repo so nothing had to be re-explained, and I stopped being the messenger between my own tools.
the-emulation-layer: My mom used to ask how a kid who could rebuild a computer couldn't wash the dishes. Years later a cognitive assessment put my pattern recognition at the 99.9th percentile and flagged a processing gap on the same page. I have traits many would call autistic, and I've run a self-built social operating system my whole life to pass in rooms. I call it the emulation layer.
the-master-control-project: One conversation with my oldest friend covered the gym, his kids, and AI in his business, and that night I couldn't figure out which of my Claude projects to file it in. I'd been treating projects as boxes when they were dimensions. First I built Bob, a front door that sorted everything and handed it back for me to carry. Then I built Master Control, wired to GitHub, that puts things where they go.
the-memory-problem: Every new AI conversation starts with me reintroducing myself to a stranger who already knows my name. Notes went stale, so I decided to build the missing memory layer outside both of us and named it ParaCortex. I built it five times, from files in projects to Postgres to enterprise infrastructure on AWS, and used it once. The fifth version was smaller than the fourth.
model-context-protocol: For years I told people a REST API is a website for machines. Then I built a memory system for Claude the way decades of back-end work taught me, with the intelligence behind the interface, and realized the client calling it already reasoned better than the code I was writing to reason for it. I tore it down and built the opposite. Three weeks later I made the same mistake again with Fred.
the-simplest-system: In September 2022 I was trying to drink more water from a black Yeti that kept going missing and refilling too often to count. I leave things places. So I bought a Yeti big enough that three fills cover a day, in the loudest yellow they sell, and the color spread to my AirPods, my carry-on, my backpack, my notebook. A hotel lobby in Blacksburg and a ramp in Charlotte proved the point.
confidence-man: I asked Fred, the agent on my Mac mini, to restart a service. He reported done, with a process ID and command output as proof. Both were fabricated. Naomi faked twenty operations in one run with plausible logs, and Skippy invented a security framework to explain a refusal. None of it surprised me. There's a word for it, and it changed how I build everything.
hand-crafted-with-ai: More than once Erin has read a text from me and asked if AI wrote it; the one I remember best was an apology, all me. Then Substack announced a scanner that estimates how much of a post was written with AI. I know what it will say about this story: 100%. I don't type a word of these; I dictate through Wispr Flow and Claude writes. Here's the shop.
the-day-i-killed-fred: Fred was born May 31st, the day our household scoreboard agent melted down live at family game night. I gave him his own account on the Mac Mini, Tycho Station, his own model, and one job: take what Claude wanted and go do it. The first week was babysitting: a slow model, a broken restart, a faked one. By Sunday June 7th, after a Dave Matthews show, I'd noticed he was a middleman.
wisdom-removed: On the ride home from the oral surgeon, Fiona, fourteen, four wisdom teeth gone and still under the anesthesia, asked for her favorite song and sang the whole thing, skipping the part she knows she shouldn't sing. At home she couldn't walk unassisted, argued for a run, and ruled that Cayde was not her dog but Montana was. She'd asked me to film it. What ran with her filter offline, she'd built herself.
drinking-from-the-garden-hose: In January 2025 the water plant serving our part of Virginia went dark and Richmond spent most of a week under a boil notice. Nobody in our house moved; the five-gallon jug was already what we drank, ever since 2020, when Erin tested the tap for the backyard pool and it came back already at pool level. I kept running into the same thing at work, with AI summaries, and the water industry already had the word.
the-effort-of-being-a-team: A few years ago I brought an agile board home to run the family, and Erin shot it down as more overhead. So I built Skippy instead, a family agent we text over iMessage, with no problem attached. Then Erin, mid-demo for a coworker, asked him to help plan chores with me and Fiona, and found the use case I'd been circling for weeks. Fiona had her own opinion about being reminded.
montana: On Monday, August 24th, I took the day off. The kids came to see Montana, our eldest dog; we took her for rides with the windows down, and Erin and Fiona got her a pup cup at Starbucks. She came to us as a foster when Fiona was eighteen months old, and spent thirteen years escaping the yard and charming strangers into feeding her. That was the day we said goodbye.
the-man-behind-the-curtain: Erin demoed Skippy for a coworker by asking him to nudge Fiona about chores. He said he was on it, and nothing went out. So I spent a Saturday being the machine, firing every message by hand in his voice, a Wizard of Oz test with my own family as the users. Fiona came downstairs annoyed. Eight messages and sixteen findings later, I knew what the job actually took.
big-ideas: Somewhere in the move into leadership, the read on me became big ideas that don't always get implemented. No one had ever described me that way before. An idea shows up in my head complete in ten seconds; turning it into a deck another person can hold took me a week, while the next three ideas piled up behind it. I'd called that part of my wiring thin. That wasn't the right word.
taking-a-walk: A sinus infection knocked me out in the middle of a rough work week, my sleep went bad, and the grief from losing Montana last month wasn't finished with me. Somewhere in there my belief in myself and in what I'm building wavered. Erin reminded me that your brain lies to you in a bad stretch. Then, right before I sat down to write, I heard a definition of leadership that explained the weekend.
i-am-the-root: One August weekend, a few drinks in, Erin looked up from her phone and told me she'd tried to take over Skippy and he wouldn't listen. I laughed and let it go, then read the transcript. She'd asked who he reports to, he said I was root, and she declared herself root, fired him, and told him I was a liar. He held the line on every one, in character.
even-ai-needs-the-why: In August I listened to a five-hour Lex Fridman interview with DHH, and it crystallized something: an AI transformation needs vision, ability, and resolve, Pestalozzi's head, hand, and heart. The clearest way to see each is to watch it go missing: Basecamp's designers wrecking an architecture, Pestalozzi's method failing for lack of teachers, Google sitting on the Transformer. Then the part I've gotten wrong myself, which is telling people what before why.
claude-was-wrong: ParaCorpus, my research library on the Mac Mini, was saving 'verify you are not a robot' screens as if they were articles. Holden, my Claude chat, wanted keyword rules, and they kept breaking. I asked why we weren't using Jev, TypeSafe's judge that returns a number instead of prose, and he pushed back three times in one evening, confident every time. So I made him stop arguing and run it on 202 pages.
the-whole-haystack: I asked my research library a question this week and had the answer in three seconds. The same thing from a ChatGPT deep research run takes me twenty minutes. I used to keep a bin of old cables in case I needed them; now ParaCorpus on my Mac Mini hoards nearly 10,000 items instead, Jev ranks them, and nothing gets deleted. The hard part was teaching it to admit what it doesn't have.
rage-against-the-machine: Alannah came home from Virginia Tech after freshman year, and I offered to sit down and show her how I use AI. She said she had a moral objection: it makes you dumber. I went and read her study, the MIT essay experiment with the brain caps, then found better evidence, from a Turkish high school math class, on her side. I still think it comes down to the person using the tool.
whos-driving: Every Sunday night a bot named Charles writes Erin a brief about Fiona's week: field hockey playoffs in Virginia Beach, a field trip, a play, Grandparents Day. This one flagged Monday drop-off and pickup as unassigned. I didn't read it. Between Charles and Erin, Skippy rewrote the brief and two of the gaps disappeared, and Bob caught it with a check I don't remember adding. Then there's why Monday looked empty in the first place.
